title: Defensive Design
purpose: Preserve original Code First and model answer, previous-learning content, original exam questions/answers/visuals and original challenge prior to replacing archived exam questions in teacher preview; ordinary student lesson source unchanged.

code_first.code:
attempts = 3
if attempts >= 3 then
    print("Locked")
else
    print("Try again")
endif
p: Explain your predicted result using the first assignment or test.
Extend to increment attempts on an incorrect password.
code_first.a: Locked; Try again; attempts = attempts + 1 when incorrect.

original_exam_questions: State two defensive programming techniques. [2 marks]
Input validation and restricted access or appropriate sanitisation; any two justified techniques.
Explain why meaningful variable names aid maintainability. [2 marks]
They make purpose easier to understand and reduce debugging/maintenance effort.
Explain why showing a user's actual password in an error message is unsafe. [2 marks]
It exposes a secret to observers and can enable unauthorised access.

optional_original_challenge.coreHint: The condition uses >= so three failed attempts trigger the lock.

stretch.task: Extend the program to show 'Warning' at exactly two failed attempts and 'Locked' at three or more.
stretch.hint: Check higher threshold first, then the lower one.
stretch.answer: IF attempts >= 3 -> Locked; ELSE IF attempts == 2 -> Warning; else Try again.

mastery.task: Adapt the program to reset the failure counter after a successful login, but not disclose the password. Give test cases for a wrong attempt followed by a success.
mastery.hint: Maintain attempts separately from a Boolean success flag.
mastery.answer: On success: attempts=0 and print a generic success message. On failure: increment attempts, lock at >=3. Test 2 failures+success -> reset; 3 failures -> locked; never print a secret.
